en: Beijing is no cheap place;
When told, it holds such turmoil.
It has peoples of many kinds,
And among those peoples
Are the accursed Kalcha lions.
Their language cannot be understood;
They have babbling speech.
One Chinese tribe
Has a single eye as large as a bucket.
While my bloodthirsty lord lived,
In the city of Kakan-Chyn,
With my lion prince at our head,
When we besieged and drove them,
Plundering their wives and daughters,
When the dear Kyrgyz took them,
Kara-Shaar and Kambyl—
Here am I, Bakai, who besieged them;
Making their Kaldai crack beneath the blows,
Here am I, Bakai, who beat him.
Laying tribute upon them, their gold—
Here am I, Bakai, who took it!
In Beijing beyond Solomon's reach,
Exacting judgment there,
Here am I, Bakai, who stood!
To Beijing beyond Alexander's reach,
While Manas of old lived,
My deeds reached that people.
I plundered their daughters
And destroyed many of their craftsmen.
I did not behold the face of Judgment Day;
While my mighty one lived,
I did not die in those days.
I passed on, a dear young man;
While my hero Manas lived,
What deeds did this dear head not do!
When we besieged the khagan's innermost city,
I did not die;
When we smashed and beat
Its stony warriors, I did not die.
When my appointed time came in Beijing,
While I stood exacting judgment,
I saw the sacred power
Of radiance-pouring Beijing;
Even there I did not die!
Of Beijing's forty gates,
When I looked upon one gate,
It opened toward our homeland.
Closed by day, by day it opened;
Closed again, again it opened.
Upon the face of that gate
The white prophet Mustafa—
The name Muhammad was written.
Lest one devil strike
The followers of Muhammad,
God's light was shed
Upon teeming Beijing.
Beijing is no easy place;
Do not put your uncle to shame—
They are no people for sport!
When I was drunk with spirits,
When I was young and broad-chested,
Parted from my elder Ala,
I returned maimed;
Parted from Khan Chubak,
I returned diminished!
My wing, my Khan Manas,
I let that swine Khan Kongurbai
Catch us unawares.
Such is the nature of battle;
In the course of fighting,
I was parted from my Syrgak!
Your aged uncle Bakai,
Parted from his gray wolf,
His chest remains rattling.
How shall I scout the road
Of the teeming Chinese,
My eyes left festering?
With my hair-thin beard grown white,
Do not torment me, my orphan,
At the time I am bound for Judgment Day!
Do not bring turmoil upon Beijing;
If you face the khagan and go,
Against the grim Black Chinese,
If we enter straight and wage war,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
If we exhaust one another,
Choose a people to serve as support;
For the face-to-face battle,
Choose your support from among heroes!
Leave the many and choose the one;
Choose one fit to be a tiger against foes,
A champion who knows the enemy's stratagems!
When the black gun cracks,
Choose a warrior who will not flee;
When the fierce gun snaps,
Choose a hero who will not flinch!
My foal, my son, if you heed me,
If you go to Beijing, go this way:
Take a marksman who shoots the eye,
Bull-necked and camel-thighed,
Who ruins those who grapple him;
Take the exceptional man who does not turn from death!
Who shoots what even a bird cannot reach;
Gather coats bullets cannot pierce.
Gather an army by calling every father's son;
Gather no small force, but a great one!
Against infidels like black worms,
If you grapple, grapple thus;
Against hero Khan Kongurbai,
If you wage war, wage it thus.
Let this year pass over you,
Then go in the following year!
Send word and let us gather
Kanykey's remedies;
Let us fatten fully
All the thoroughbred chargers.
Let the horse grow fat and ready;
Let the hero grow stout and pent with force;
Then go to Beijing!
Your father Manas was a lion;
I was his uncle Bakai,
Who never crossed what he said.
I was Bakai who wore
A bulletproof iron shield!
I was Bakai who knew
Kakan-Chyn's Beijing!
Traveling on campaign for six months,
Going no little way, but far,
To Chinmachin's khagan—
Those people are Chinese of ancient stock,
Their multitude thick as black worms.
The more depleted, the more they smoldered;
They are a people rooted deep.
Fighting until all were exhausted—
Know that I am that Bakai!
The more they died, the more they multiplied;
They are those accursed Chinese people.
My roar splitting stones,
Parted from my own companion,
I am the one now going toward death!
Know this grief of mine!
My only one left by the lion,
Grant me this journey and heed me!
Beijing is no easy place;
The Chinese are a fierce and unruly people,
No people from whom five or six riders
Can exact vengeance!
It has a pass on which it relies,
And a place lying fortified.
Broad-booted and cotton-sashed,
Kongurbai, khan of the Kechil,
It has that swaggering lion.
He still lives, neither dead nor gone;
Bakai has words to tell of him.
Do not act imperiously, my foal;
The ill-starred bloodthirsty man
Has black eyes watching.
What your father destroyed,
What your lion accomplished,
Inscribed in its register.
When the following year comes,
Take male camels from the herds,
Take plenty of every kind of equipment,
Take a full count of the army,
And enter the army on the rolls.
Leaving out no able-bodied man,
Let us gather them all!
Making the face of the earth thunder,
Then let us go to Beijing!
Those who go on holy war may die;
The brave scout will reconnoiter the road.
So the people who go need burden no one,
And their lice do not multiply,
Let us prepare underclothing;
To enter battle fully equipped,
To strike the foe without tiring,
Let us ready armor against bullets!
The Chinese inhabit Beijing,
Whose heat gives no respite.
Beijing is no easy place;
For every man let us prepare
A coat with golden collar and copper sleeves,
For him to cast himself against the foe,
To stand fighting the enemy,
To extend his spear without fleeing—
Let it be a coat bullets cannot pierce.
Who then will have great regret,
If we stand and fight without fleeing,
And bring great conflict upon the Kakan?
If we stand face to face,
Clashing and hewing with swords,
Bathed in red blood,
Standing amid slaughter,
Swallowing the Kara-Khan,
If we stand and fight without fleeing.
So we do not die by the sword,
So untimely death does not reach us,
Your dear father's contemporary,
That confidant Bölökbai—
When he worked the bellows, it stirred;
Döötü and Bölökbai
Were friends for the world beyond.
Skilled in every kind of object,
What Bölökbai made,
He and Döötü together
Made after taking counsel.
With Bölökbai at their head,
Let us prepare eighty smiths;
Helmets of blue steel,
To be set upside down upon the head,
So all the ready warriors
May strike the foe without tiring;
Let us make mail-cap helmets,
Let us ready the weapons of war.
Let us take an exact count
Of the troops going to the Kakan!
Against the seething unbelievers,
Against hero Khan Kongurbai,
Thus let us begin the conflict!
Wearing coats without a hole,
Gathering an army fit to match them,
Let us take the host together,
My splendid young hero,
And ride thus into battle!
Preparing troops of many kinds,
For the force going to exchange fire,
Preparing abundant provisions.
My horses on the hills are piebald,
Swift horses and chargers mixed together.
There are well-fattened mares;
Choose and slaughter the fat ones,
Have the servants butcher them,
And select provisions.
If you bring great conflict upon China,
So the army does not go hungry,
Let us firmly prepare journey-rations!
If we wage battle against Beijing!
Let us not be caught unawares!
If we set out for Kakan-Chin,
Let dust fly into the sky,
As the army gathers in a mass.
The spearheads clashing,
Each intending to go on holy war,
The army racing with a roar.
While your lion father lived,
He chose seven heroes,
Stationed them in seven places,
Had them called sons of the accomplished,
Brought great conflict upon Beijing,
And ravaged every place they reached.
All the fine-bred horses,
He made prance in the mountains;
The seething Chinese,
He made their wives and daughters weep,
And destroyed the cities
Of the black Chinese and Manchu.
